slides.title: Me, and a website about circuits
slides.subtitle: The version they don't put on the LinkedIn banner

slides.title: The UG project: mining Bitcoin on a Raspberry Pi
slides.caption: Jan–Apr 2022. Hash rate: modest. Enthusiasm: not modest at all.

box.content: Before RFID readers, there was this: a final-year project asking whether a Raspberry Pi could mine cryptocurrency without bankrupting a student.

list.text: Raspberry Pi as the controller, running open-source mining software — no ASIC, no budget for one.
Power vs. payout, tuned by hand — that trade-off was the actual research question, not the mining itself.
Verdict: technically works, economically hilarious. The electricity bill won.
First real lesson in low-cost hardware experimentation — the instinct that led to everything after.

note.text: This is also the honest origin story of "guy who writes hardware tutorials for a living."

slides.title: Four boards, four very different jobs
slides.caption: The flex check, ranked. Yes, someone put gold chains on a Jetson Nano.

list.title: ESP32
list.text: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth built in, dirt cheap, dual-core. Default pick for anything that needs to talk to the internet.

list.title: Arduino
list.text: The one that just works. No OS, no surprises — perfect for a sensor that reads a value and does one thing well.

list.title: Raspberry Pi
list.text: A real Linux box small enough to hide in a project box. Ran the mining rig above; runs actual servers now.

list.title: Jetson Nano
list.text: GPU on a board — the one you reach for when "AI" has to run on the device itself, not in the cloud.

note.text: Circuit Digest's tutorials cover all four. Pick the board that matches the job, not the one that's trending.

slides.title: My actual job for 2.5 years (no glamour)
slides.caption: Pushed on Friday at 5 PM. Shocked when it broke. Every single time.

box.content: The CV says "integrated RFID systems." The reality was more like:

list.text: 150+ production fires put out, mostly at hours that shouldn't exist.
Byte-level UID and CSN wrestling — because two readers from two vendors will never, ever agree on endianness.
RS-232 timeouts that worked perfectly in the lab and only failed on-site, only on Fridays, only when I had plans.
SQL deadlocks under load, sync that ate transactions, and a thermal printer that had opinions about paper width.

note.text: None of this was in any tutorial. All of it is what the actual job looks like.

slides.title: So what even is Circuit Digest?
slides.caption: The actual feature graphic. SMS alerts, plate reads, barcode scans, GPS pins. All real.

box.title: circuitdigest.com — published by Semicon Media, Coimbatore

list.text: One of the most-read electronics and embedded publications on the internet. Seriously.
Build guides for Arduino, ESP32, Raspberry Pi, STM32 — real circuits, real code, actual photos of messy breadboards.
Datasheets translated into human language, and hardware reviews that aren't just "it's great!" five times.
Read by students, hobbyists, and engineers who Google things at midnight in more countries than I can count.

slides.title: Circuit Digest Cloud — what I actually build now
slides.imageAlt: Cartoon of a tiny ESP32 chip lifting a barbell of data up to a smiling cloud
slides.caption: An ESP32 has about 320 KB of RAM. This is roughly how the upload feels.
slides.content:
Tutorials are one half. Infrastructure is the other.

Circuit Digest Cloud handles: device provisioning and fleet management, MQTT telemetry with live dashboards, and alerts over email, SMS, and WhatsApp. You know, the fun stuff that breaks at 3 AM.

And it isn't a black box — the client libraries (GeoLinker, the WhatsApp API examples for half a dozen boards) are open source on GitHub. You can read exactly what gets sent over the wire.

slides.title: This is the actual product, not a mockup
slides.caption: No Figma screenshot. This is circuitdigest.cloud, live, as of yesterday.

box.content:
135 projects active in the last 24 hours. 249 weekly active users. 6,331 community members building stuff with it.

"One platform to analyse, control, and connect" — that's the real tagline. I didn't make it up for this slide, I promise.

Every feature here is a documented HTTPS endpoint under circuitdigest.cloud/api/v1/ — the same API a hobbyist hits from an Arduino Uno is the one running this dashboard. No separate "enterprise" backend hiding behind it.

slides.title: The stack (minus the buzzwords)
slides.caption: Not pictured: Circuit Digest Cloud, which stayed with FastAPI and didn't even look twice.

list.text: FastAPI + PostgreSQL + MQTT doing the heavy lifting for ingestion and device APIs.
GPS tracking with polygon geofencing and maps that actually update in real time.
Computer vision for number plates, helmets, objects, plus live video. Yes, on an ESP32.
Deployed on DigitalOcean with GitHub Actions and Sentry catching the 2 AM surprises before I do.

slides.title: Every API in the catalog, for real
slides.caption: The actual catalog page. Nine computer-vision models, three messaging channels, one GPS tracker. Scroll, don't imagine.

list.text: SMS, Email, WhatsApp — three notification APIs, each a single HTTPS POST with a template ID and a phone number or address.
Nine computer-vision endpoints — number plates, helmets, faces, parking spaces, waste sorting, currency, even 35-class hand gestures. Point a camera, get JSON back.
AI Vision Analyst — describes a scene or extracts text from a photo, built for ESP32-CAM and Raspberry Pi camera modules.
GeoLinker — the GPS tracking API from the next slide, same catalog, same auth.

note.text: Every one of these is free to call, no credit card at sign-up. That's not a typo.

slides.title: GeoLinker — this is real GPS, not a screenshot
slides.caption: A real tracker on a real walk around Coimbatore. 7.18 km, 26 minutes. My feet hurt.

box.content:
GeoLinker is the GPS tracking piece of Circuit Digest Cloud: live position, route history, and polygon geofencing, plotted on an actual map.

This is not a mockup. One of our trackers, walking the streets near our office. I was the one walking.

list.text: Open-source Arduino library — five method calls (setApiKey, setDeviceID, setUpdateInterval_seconds, setPayloads, loop) and a JSON POST to /api/v1/geolinker is the whole integration.
Works over Wi-Fi or SIM800L cellular, and buffers up to 100 GPS points locally when the connection drops — syncs the moment it's back.
Runs on ESP32, ESP8266, Arduino Uno R4 WiFi, or a Raspberry Pi Pico W — the same lineup from the boards slide, doing actual work.

slides.title: The board GeoLinker actually runs on
slides.caption: Yes, that's a Pac-Man animation etched into the antenna trace. Someone had fun with this one.

box.content: Not a rendering — a real product on the Circuit Digest wiki. ESP32 and cellular GPS on one board, small enough to hide inside anything that moves.

list.text: ESP32-S3-MINI-1 + SIM868 — dual-core 240 MHz, paired with a quad-band GSM/GPRS modem for when Wi-Fi isn't an option.
GPS + GLONASS + BeiDou baked in, so it gets a fix almost anywhere, not just where GPS satellites feel generous.
~10 µA deep sleep with motion-triggered wake — it can sit dormant on a parked vehicle for weeks.
33 × 85 mm, LiPo charging, accelerometer, RGB status LED — everything an asset tracker needs, nothing it doesn't.

note.text: This is the board behind the Coimbatore walk from two slides ago. Full pinout and build guide live on the Circuit Digest wiki.

slides.title: And yes, we also built a drone
slides.caption: 45 grams, four motors, one ESP32. Flies better than most of my side projects.

box.content: LiteWing: an open-hardware, Wi-Fi-controlled quadcopter, because at some point "IoT device" stopped being enough of a challenge.

list.text: ESP32-S3 flight controller talking CRTP over Wi-Fi — the same protocol Crazyflie drones use.
~45 g, 100 × 100 mm, four coreless motors. Light enough that a crash is a shrug, not a funeral.
Flown from a phone app, a Python SDK, or the Arduino IDE — pick your level of "how much do I want to debug today."
Optional barometer, ToF, and optical-flow modules add altitude hold and position hold — on a drone marketed as one of the cheapest DIY kits out there.

note.text: Marketed as one of the most affordable DIY drones around. It is also, unfortunately, extremely fun to crash.

slides.title: From jumper wires to a working dashboard
slides.caption: ESP32, a SIM800L, a fistful of jumper wires, and a phone proving it actually works.

box.content:
This is the whole job, honestly. A breadboard held together with hope and rubber bands on one side, a live map with your data on the other.

Everything in the tools section exists to make the wiring side faster. Not to replace it. You still need to know which wire goes where.

None of this is locked away, either — the public example repos on GitHub wire up the exact same thing: an ultrasonic sensor triggering a WhatsApp alert on an Arduino Uno R4, a Raspberry Pi Pico W doing the same over Wi-Fi. Clone one, swap the sensor, ship your own.

slides.title: The dashboard nobody believes is real
slides.caption: Live camera, live chart, live controls. This is not a template. It's our product.

box.content:
Colour pickers for the lights, a slider and gauge for room temperature, a WebRTC camera feed, and a 24-hour chart — all updating from actual MQTT messages sent by actual hardware sitting on someone's desk.

Each widget subscribes to its own MQTT topic and repaints the instant a message lands. No polling, no refresh button, no "last updated 5 minutes ago" lie.

slides.title: We already put an AI in it (yes, on WhatsApp)
slides.caption: "Which of my devices are offline?" It just answers. At 3 AM. Without complaining.

box.content: Circuit Digest Cloud ships this in v0.1.1: an MCP server that lets Claude or ChatGPT connect straight to your account, plus a WhatsApp bot that checks device status, reads telemetry, sends commands, and manages automations — all in plain English. It even adjusts to IST without being asked.

slides.title: How it's actually wired together (no magic)
slides.caption: The same API catalog from three slides ago. Turns out the AI uses the front door too.

box.content: No, it doesn't have a password to the database. That would be a security slide, not a feature slide.

list.text: Claude is the reasoning layer — it reads your WhatsApp message and decides what to check.
MCP tools stand in for raw database access — get device status, pull telemetry, list what's offline. The model calls a tool, never a table.
MQTT → ingestion → Postgres keeps those tools honest. Ask "is it online," get an answer from seconds ago, not a stale cache.
WhatsApp is just the transport. The model has no idea it's WhatsApp — it just answers with whatever tools it's handed.

note.text: Which is a convenient place to stop talking about our product and start talking about how this magic became possible at all.

topics.title: From autocomplete to whatever this is

slides.title: From autocomplete to whatever this is
slides.subtitle: A short, very opinionated history

slides.title: Four years, four entirely different vibes
slides.caption: The last panel is not a joke. Someone in this room will do this by Friday.

list.text: Autocomplete era (2021): TabNine, early GitHub Copilot. It finished your line. Sometimes even the right one.
Chat era (2022): ChatGPT shows up in November. You asked, it answered, you copy-pasted and hoped for the best.
Editor copilots (2023): Copilot Chat, Cursor. It moved into the IDE. Could see your file. Still couldn't see your pain.
Agent era (2024–now): Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity. It reads the repo, runs the tests, reads the errors, sulks, and tries again.

slides.title: A chatbot vs an agent (finally, a clear answer)
leftPoints: You copy, paste, wire it up yourself
Great for learning and getting unstuck
One turn at a time — you drive everything
rightPoints: Reads files, runs commands, edits code directly
Plans, acts, checks its own work, fixes its own mess
Can read docs and confirm what it did actually works
Chases a goal across many steps without you babysitting

note.text: Claude Code, Antigravity, and Codex are all in the right column. So are the new open-weight agentic models out of China — DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen. This isn't a closed-lab thing anymore.

slides.title: The colleague who never sleeps and never brings snacks
slides.imageAlt: A frazzled four-armed robot coding at 2:47 AM surrounded by coffee cups
slides.caption: 2:47 AM. Fourth coffee. "Project: almost done." It is absolutely not almost done.
slides.content:
The word that matters is agency

A chatbot can explain a bug. An agent opens the file, reproduces the bug, patches it, runs the suite, and hands you a diff. Same brain underneath. Completely different thing to work with.

The newest ones don't even stay inside the editor — they can open a browser, click through a real UI, and operate a computer the way you would. "Never brings snacks" is doing less exaggerating than it used to.

slides.title: Hot take (I will die on this hill)
slides.caption: "Sleep is optional." "Deploy on Friday." This wall is the argument FOR AI, not against it.

box.content:
Most "AI will replace developers" posts are written by people who have never been paged at 3 AM to fix a data migration.

The job was never typing. It's deciding what to build, and being the person who understands the system when everything is on fire. AI moves the typing. It does not move the responsibility.

The same week GPT-6 Astra became the first model rated "Critical" for cybersecurity capability, someone still had to decide whether to let it anywhere near production. That decision doesn't automate. It never will.

slides.title: Adoption, roughly (no fake chart, I promise)
slides.caption: Every AI keynote has this exact chart. Here's ours. For compliance.

box.content:
I could show you a real adoption number. You'd forget it by the next slide. So here's the honest version:

In 2022, using AI at work was a party trick. In 2026, not using it is the thing that gets a raised eyebrow in code review. That's the whole trend. You're welcome.

slides.title: The skill that actually matters now
slides.caption: "Algorithms and Suffering" is not a real book. But it should be. Fundamentals still win.

list.text: Prompting — giving enough context so it doesn't hallucinate your database schema. Paste the actual schema. It isn't psychic.
Verifying — reading AI output like you'd review a pull request from a confident new hire. Run it, don't just skim it.
Security sense — not pasting your .env file into the chat. You'd be surprised how many people do.
Knowing when to stop it — three failed attempts at the same bug means the approach is wrong, not the fourth prompt. Close the session, start fresh.

topics.title: Using it without making a mess

slides.title: Using it without making a mess
slides.subtitle: Where it helps, where it lies, and how to ask nicely

slides.title: The old loop vs the new loop
slides.caption: "PROJECT CHAOS (DOOMED)." This is the old loop. Unfiltered. Undefeated.

list.text: Old: plan, write, test, review, deploy — every step by hand. Writing an ESP32 driver from a 40-page datasheet used to eat an entire afternoon.
New: same steps, but an agent drafts that driver from the datasheet PDF in minutes. You still verify every register address against the actual chip. That part doesn't automate.

slides.title: Where it's genuinely useful vs where it's a confident liar
leftPoints: Boilerplate and scaffolding (finally, someone else writes the Dockerfile)
Explaining a codebase you were just handed 20 minutes ago
First-draft tests for code that already works
Debugging with a real stack trace in hand
rightPoints: Architecture — it'll pick one and defend it with zero shame
Security review — misses the subtle holes, cheerfully
Domain judgement — it doesn't know your users or your weird edge cases
"Is this actually correct?" — only you and the tests can answer that

note.text: It is never unsure. That's the dangerous part. It will be wrong with perfect grammar.

slides.title: Time saved, honestly (no fake percentage, I promise)
slides.caption: The bottom-right panel is not hypothetical. It happens. Budget time for it.

box.content: I could give you a made-up "40% faster" number. Here's the honest breakdown instead:

list.text: Genuinely faster: boilerplate, scaffolding, first-draft tests. Minutes instead of a copy-paste archaeology dig.
About the same: debugging with a real stack trace. You get to a fix faster, but reading it critically still takes the time it always took.
Not faster at all: architecture and judgement calls. You still think. You just argue with something first.
New cost that didn't exist before: reviewing plausible-but-wrong code you didn't write. Nobody puts that in the pitch deck.

note.text: A session costs cents to a few dollars in tokens. That was never the real price. The discipline to review everything is.

slides.title: Bad prompt vs good prompt (same request, very different afternoon)

box.title: One of these ruins your day. The other saves it.
box.code:
// Vague - invites guessing and sadness
"fix my code"

// Specific - grounded in reality
"In src/api/users.py, GET /users/{id} returns 500
when id is not numeric. Traceback below. Add
validation that returns 400 with a clear message,
matching validate_order_id() in src/api/orders.py.
<paste traceback>"

slides.title: Before you let it anywhere near the main branch
slides.caption: This is not a workflow diagram. It's a confession with rounded corners.

list.text: Read every single line. Don't merge what you haven't actually read. Yes, all of it.
Actually run it. Don't just nod at it like you're reviewing a wedding invitation.
Grep for keys, tokens, and hardcoded credentials. The AI loves to help with those too.
Be able to explain it — in a code review, in a viva, in a job interview. If you can't, it's not yours.

note.text: Rule of thumb: if you'd be embarrassed to have written it, don't ship it under your name.

slides.title: The human stays in the loop (this is not optional)
slides.imageAlt: A team meeting where the whiteboard reads AI DO NOT TOUCH MAIN BRANCH and a cheerful robot says I CAN DO THAT
slides.caption: The whiteboard says don't touch main. The robot says "I can do that." Your job is to stand between them.
slides.content:
Every workflow in this talk has a human checkpoint

That's not overcaution. It's the line between using AI as a power tool and quietly outsourcing your judgement to a thing that can't feel embarrassment.

Even the tools agree, technically: Claude Code's own recent updates added managed MCP servers and stricter headless permission controls specifically so a human stays the one approving what an agent is allowed to touch.

slides.title: The actual tools
slides.subtitle: What each one does, and when you should actually reach for it

slides.title: Six tools, six different jobs
slides.caption: The temptation is real. Finish the current project FIRST.

list.text: ESP-IDF — the framework your ESP32 firmware actually runs on.
GitHub — repos, CI/CD, and where all these AI tools plug in.
Google Antigravity — Google DeepMind's agentic IDE. It's as wild as it sounds.
OpenAI Codex — OpenAI's cloud agent. Does the work, hands you a PR.
Claude Code — Anthropic's terminal agent. Lives in your shell. Judges your code.
Open-weight models — DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen, GLM. Chinese labs closed the coding gap fast: Kimi K3 leads the frontend-code benchmarks, DeepSeek V4 is MIT-licensed and self-hostable on your own GPU.

slides.title: ESP-IDF — where the firmware actually lives
slides.imageAlt: Isometric cartoon of a circuit board drawn as a small town called Microville
slides.caption: Welcome to Microville. Population: 1024 bytes. Every IoT project starts in a town like this.
slides.content:
Espressif's official SDK for ESP32-class chips

  • Built on FreeRTOS — real multitasking on a chip smaller than your thumbnail.
  • idf.py to build and flash, menuconfig for when you want to feel like a Linux kernel dev.
  • JTAG and OpenOCD for real debugging, not serial-print archaeology.

slides.title: GitHub — boring, essential, and it runs everything

list.text: Repos and pull requests — where code review actually happens (or doesn't, and then things break).
Actions — the pipeline that deploys Circuit Digest Cloud. Every push. Automatically. While I sleep.
Copilot — inline autocomplete that sometimes reads your mind, and sometimes suggests importing a library you uninstalled three commits ago.
Copilot coding agent — assign it an issue like you would a teammate, and it opens its own PR. GitHub isn't just where the AI tools plug in anymore; it's becoming one.

slides.title: Before you start vibe coding (please read this first)
slides.imageAlt: Holographic software blueprints including PRD, User Flow, Architecture, and AI Rules on a modern development workspace
slides.caption: Specs and blueprints anchor the agent before it starts generating code and opinions.

box.title: Four documents, with real examples from GeoLinker

list.title: PRD
list.text: What to build, and why, in one unambiguous sentence. GeoLinker's: "alert the owner within 30 seconds of a tracker leaving its saved polygon."

list.title: User Flow
list.text: How a human actually gets there: open dashboard → draw polygon → save → get a WhatsApp alert on exit. If you can't draw it in five boxes, you don't understand the feature yet.

list.title: Tech Spec
list.text: The boring part that saves you later: geofence checks run server-side on every MQTT ping, not on the ESP32. Battery life mattered more than shaving off milliseconds.

list.title: AI Coding Rules
list.text: The boundaries: never touch the alerts pipeline without a human review, never invent a new table without asking first. Claude Code reads this file every session.

note.text: The other six — detailed User Flow diagrams, UI/UX, DB Schema, API Spec, Security Rules, Testing Plan — still matter. They just don't fit on one slide.

slides.title: Codex & Antigravity in 60 seconds (timer starts now)

list.title: OpenAI Codex
list.text: Cloud + CLI agent. Runs in an isolated sandbox with its own copy of the repo, does the work, hands it back as a PR. Point it at "add rate limiting to the telemetry ingestion endpoint," walk away, come back to a diff and a test file.

list.title: Google Antigravity
list.text: Agentic IDE with browser sub-agents that open your actual running UI, click around it, and screenshot the result — not just guess from the CSS. Ask it to fix a broken dashboard layout and it verifies the fix visually before handing it back.

note.text: Codex just got sharper teeth: OpenAI's new flagship, GPT-6 Astra, is state-of-the-art on coding and computer use — and the first model OpenAI itself rates "Critical" for cybersecurity capability. Reviewing the diff matters more than ever, not less.

slides.title: Claude Code — the one that lives in your terminal

list.text: Reads your files, edits them, and runs your commands directly. No copy-paste. It just does it.
MCP lets it plug into external tools and data sources. Databases, APIs, whatever you connect.
Plan mode proposes a plan for you to approve before it touches a single line. Trust but verify, etc.
Shipping fast — managed MCP servers, a plugin eval framework, and desktop panes you can pop out and dock back all landed within weeks of each other. Current release as of mid-September: v2.1.270.

note.text: Full disclosure: this deck was built with Claude Code. In this repo. It's eating its own dog food.

slides.title: Making it actually yours: CLAUDE.md and Skills
slides.caption: How deep does this rabbit hole go? Deeper than you'd guess.

list.title: CLAUDE.md
list.text: A plain file at the repo root: conventions, commands, things it should never touch. Read every session, so you stop repeating yourself.

list.title: Skills
list.text: Packaged instructions for a specific job, like a slash command. This deck's slides were built by one — /add-presentation.

list.title: Personas
list.text: Goes further still: this deck was written under a plugin called "Ponytail" (laziest working solution, question every abstraction) paired with "Caveman" (short, blunt sentences, no fluff). Both real. Both installed.

note.text: If you were wondering why this talk has zero corporate padding, now you know why.

slides.title: 6 ways to shoot yourself in the foot with Claude Code
slides.subtitle: Learn from our mistakes so you don't have to make your own

list.title: Don't dump the entire spec in one go.
list.text: It overwhelms the session and buries what matters. Break it into phases. Feed one at a time. Like eating — don't shove the whole pizza in.

list.title: Don't lose your prompts. Write them down.
list.text: If the session dies or you switch machines, you should never have to reconstruct instructions from memory. That's not a workflow, that's amnesia.

list.title: Don't waste context on small talk.
list.text: Every tangent, repeated explanation, and random debugging thread eats the memory it needs for your actual project. Keep sessions focused.

list.title: Don't build everything before testing anything.
list.text: Test each phase before starting the next. Small bugs left alone quietly evolve into large, angry bugs that are much harder to find.

list.title: Don't let the AI play architect.
list.text: Database design, security approach, tech stack — those decisions are yours. Claude Code should implement your calls, not make them.

list.title: Don't skip git commits. Ever.
list.text: Commit after every working milestone. One bad change without history can undo hours of progress. Git is your undo button. Use it.

note.text: Six habits, one outcome: you stay in control of the build, not the other way around.

slides.title: Free stuff nobody told you about (you're welcome)

list.text: GitHub Student Developer Pack — a genuinely large bundle of free tools (Copilot, Codespaces, Azure and DigitalOcean credit, every JetBrains IDE) for anyone with a valid student email. Verify once at education.github.com.

Open source — search "good first issue" on GitHub any day of the year, or wait for Hacktoberfest every October: four valid pull requests to opt-in repos gets you a shirt and, more usefully, a merged PR with your name on it.
Hackathons — MLH runs 150+ events a year and often covers travel for shortlisted teams. Smart India Hackathon is the government-run one, with real prize money for the national finalists.
Competitions — Google Summer of Code pays a real stipend to work on open source over a summer. Kaggle prize pools on the bigger competitions run into the tens of thousands of dollars.

note.text: Pick one. Actually do it this month. Bookmarking is not participation.

slides.title: Two more things, and then I'm done nagging

box.title: The unglamorous stuff that actually moves the needle

list.text: Contribute to one open-source project. Not a drive-by PR — pick something you actually use, stick around, learn how a real codebase reviews code.
Find a FOSS org, not just a repo. CNCF projects, Frappe, Home Assistant, whatever's in your stack. The community teaches you more than the code does.
Build a portfolio site. Doesn't need to be fancy — mine is a static GitHub Pages site, aravind-govindhasamy.github.io. A few real projects, real links, done.
Put the link everywhere. LinkedIn, resume, email signature. Nobody's impressed by a CV line. Everyone clicks a link.

note.text: A GitHub profile with real commits beats a resume PDF every single time. Recruiters actually click through.

slides.title: If you remember exactly four things from today
slides.caption: Do these four and the line goes up. Results may vary. Line not to scale.

list.text: Circuit Digest turns electronics knowledge into tutorials and real infrastructure that people actually use.
AI moved from answering questions to doing things. That's the entire story of the last two years.
Keep a human checkpoint before and after the agent acts. Every time. No exceptions.
ESP-IDF, GitHub, Antigravity, Codex, Claude Code — each solves a different slice of the problem.

slides.title: Questions? The real ones. Don't be polite.
Thank you, PSGCAS
